text: A SOC dashboard isn't a report. A report looks backward and summarizes a period that already ended; a dashboard looks at this second and tells an analyst where to point their attention next. Almost everything on it should answer one question: does this need a human to act on it right now, mid-shift, before anything else?

In practice that narrows a real dashboard down to a handful of live panels: open high-severity alerts, sorted oldest first so nothing ages out of sight; queue depth, meaning how many alerts across all severities are currently sitting unassigned, shown with a trend arrow so a growing backlog is visible before it becomes a crisis; and a short list of hosts or accounts already flagged as under active investigation, so an incoming analyst on shift handoff knows what's already in motion.

Everything else tends to be a vanity metric — total alerts processed since the SIEM went live, lifetime log volume ingested, a pie chart of every alert category ever seen. None of it is wrong or fabricated, and it can look genuinely impressive in a slide deck, but none of it changes what an analyst does in the next five minutes, which is the only real design target for a live screen.

That matters because a cluttered dashboard doesn't just look busy — it costs real response time. An analyst scanning a crowded screen for the one panel that actually matters has to visually search through the noise first, and that search time adds directly onto Mean Time to Detect, the metric Lesson 22 covers in full.

Worse, once analysts learn that the dashboard's highlighted panels are mostly noise, they stop trusting it and quietly build their own workaround instead — a saved search, a personal spreadsheet, a sticky note on the monitor. At that point the official dashboard has failed at its one job even though it's technically still running, and that's strictly worse than having no dashboard at all, because leadership believes real-time visibility exists when it doesn't.
